reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: IRB credit capital on a USD 120m loan book: PD 2%, recovery 40%, asset correlation $\rho = 0.25$. The worst-case default rate is $WCDR = N\left[\frac{N^{-1}(PD) + \sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(0.999)}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right]$, with $N^{-1}(0.02) = -2.054$ and $N^{-1}(0.999) = 3.090$.
ask: The 99.9% worst-case default rate is closest to:

options.label: About 2% (the PD itself)
options.why: Applied no stress. The 99.9% scenario is a very bad year, so WCDR must sit well above the 2% average PD; capital is charged on the gap (WCDR $-$ PD).

options.label: About 7%
options.why: Used $\rho$ instead of $\sqrt{\rho}$ in the numerator: $(-2.054 + 0.25 \times 3.090)/0.866 = -1.48$, and $N(-1.48) \approx 7\%$.

takeaway: WCDR is the PD in a one-in-a-thousand bad year, far above the average PD. Capital covers only the unexpected part, WCDR minus PD.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel II IRB. CAD 300m of drawn BB corporate loans: one-year PD 1%, LGD 30%, 99.9th-percentile default rate 14%, maturity adjustment 1.26. Risk-weighted assets are $12.5 \times EAD \times LGD \times (DR - PD) \times MA$.

options.label: ≈ CAD 15m
options.why: The capital figure ($8\%$ of RWA), not the RWA: the factor 12.5 was left out.

options.label: ≈ CAD 610m
options.why: Left out LGD: $12.5 \times 300 \times 0.13 \times 1.26$ treats every defaulted loan as a total loss.

options.label: ≈ CAD 1,850m
options.why: Scale slip (10×): a decimal point lost in $12.5 \times 300 \times 0.30$. RWA of 1,850 would be over six times the CAD 300m exposure.

takeaway: RWA is $12.5\times$ capital. A risk weight well below 100% (here about 61%) is what a 30% LGD and a 1% PD should give.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel II IRB portfolio: EAD EUR 200m, one-year expected loss EUR 4.2m, expected recovery 30%. Default rate at the 95th percentile 5.66%, at the 99.9th percentile 9.87%. Capital = worst-case loss at the IRB confidence level minus expected loss.
ask: Is the Basel II credit capital above or below EUR 12m?

options.label: Above EUR 12m
options.why: Stopped at the worst-case loss $200 \times 0.70 \times 9.87\% = 13.8$ and forgot to deduct the EUR 4.2m expected loss; leaving out LGD instead gives about 15.5, also above 12.

takeaway: IRB capital covers unexpected loss only: worst-case loss at 99.9% minus expected loss. The 95th percentile is a distractor.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel II asset correlation for bank, corporate and sovereign exposures is a blend: $\rho = 0.12\,w + 0.24\,(1-w)$, where $w = \frac{1-e^{-50\,PD}}{1-e^{-50}}$. A borrower has PD = 1%.
ask: Is $\rho$ closer to the 0.12 floor or to the 0.24 ceiling?

options.label: Closer to 0.12
options.why: Assumed a higher-risk borrower has higher correlation. The formula runs the other way: the weight on 0.12 is only $w = 0.39$ at PD = 1%, so $\rho$ leans towards 0.24.

options.label: Exactly midway
options.why: Would need $w = 0.5$, i.e. $e^{-50\,PD} = 0.5$. At PD = 1% it is $e^{-0.5} = 0.61$, so $w = 0.39$ and $\rho$ is above the midpoint 0.18.

takeaway: Basel II correlation falls as PD rises: low-PD names get correlation near 0.24, high-PD names near 0.12.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel 2.5 market risk capital uses the 10-day 99% VaR: $MR = \max(VaR_{t-1}, m\,VaR_{avg}) + \max(SVaR_{t-1}, m_s\,SVaR_{avg})$, with $m = 3.0$. 10-day VaR in USD m, previous day / 60-day average: 95% row 110 / 127; 99% row 185 / 140; 99.9% row 283 / 228.
ask: The VaR leg, $\max(VaR_{t-1},\, 3.0 \times VaR_{avg})$, is closest to:

options.label: USD 185m
options.why: Kept the previous-day VaR and ignored the multiplied average: $3.0 \times 140 = 420$ is larger and the leg takes the maximum.

options.label: USD 381m
options.why: Read the 95% row: $\max(110, 3 \times 127) = 381$. Basel 2.5 uses the 99% row.

options.label: USD 684m
options.why: Read the 99.9% row: $\max(283, 3 \times 228) = 684$. Basel 2.5 uses the 99% row.

takeaway: Basel 2.5 uses the 99% 10-day VaR. The multiplied 60-day average usually beats the previous-day figure.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel 2.5 charge: $\max(VaR_{t-1}, 3.0\,VaR_{avg}) + \max(SVaR_{t-1}, 3.5\,SVaR_{avg})$. All figures 10-day 99%, in USD: previous-day VaR 800, 60-day average VaR 360; stressed VaR, most stressful previous-day equivalent over seven years 950, most stressful 60-day average 370.

options.label: The previous-day stressed figure: 950
options.why: Took the seven-year worst-day figure at face value. The multiplied average, $3.5 \times 370 = 1{,}295$, is larger, and each leg takes the maximum.

takeaway: In each Basel 2.5 leg the multiplier (3 or more) on the 60-day average usually dominates the single previous-day figure.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel 2.5 market risk capital $= \max(VaR_{t-1}, 3\,VaR_{avg}) + \max(SVaR_{t-1}, 3\,SVaR_{avg})$, all 10-day 99%, in USD m. VaR: previous day 1.2, 60-day average 1.4. Stressed VaR: previous day 2.2, 60-day average 2.0.
ask: The capital charge is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 3.4m
options.why: Left out the multiplier of 3 and took raw figures: $1.2 + 2.2 = 3.4$ (the two averages, $1.4 + 2.0$, also give 3.4).

options.label: ≈ USD 31m
options.why: Multiplied the whole charge by 3 a second time: $3 \times 10.2 = 30.6$.

options.label: ≈ USD 102m
options.why: Scale slip (10×): a decimal place lost somewhere in the 10.2m total.

takeaway: The multiplier applies to the 60-day averages inside each max, once. Both averages (times 3) beat the previous-day figures here.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: A bank has one-day 95% VaR figures and needs the 10-day 99% VaR that Basel 2.5 uses. Returns are normal; the 95% z-value is 1.645 and the 99% z-value is 2.326.
ask: The factor that converts one-day 95% VaR to 10-day 99% VaR is closest to:

options.label: About 1.4
options.why: Scaled the confidence level only ($2.326/1.645$) and left out the time scaling.

options.label: About 3.2
options.why: Scaled the horizon only ($\sqrt{10}$) and stayed at 95% confidence.

options.label: About 14
options.why: Multiplied the confidence ratio by 10 days instead of $\sqrt{10}$: $1.414 \times 10$.

takeaway: Two separate conversions multiply: confidence level (z ratio) and horizon (square root of time).

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: NSFR $= ASF/RSF$. A bank's funding (USD m, ASF factor): stable retail deposits 80 (90%), wholesale deposits 100 (50%), Tier 2 capital 40 (100%), Tier 1 capital 80 (100%). Total funding is 300.
ask: Available stable funding (ASF) is closest to:

options.label: USD 192m
options.why: Dropped the wholesale deposits entirely: $72 + 40 + 80 = 192$. They count at 50%, not 0%.

options.label: USD 300m
options.why: Counted all funding at 100%, ignoring the ASF factors.

takeaway: ASF is funding weighted by stability, so it falls below the balance-sheet total whenever some funding is less than fully stable.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: NSFR $= ASF/RSF$ (USD m, factor). Funding: retail deposits 35 (90%), wholesale deposits 67.5 (50%), Tier 2 capital 5 (100%), Tier 1 capital 10 (100%). Assets: cash 7 (0%), mortgages 38 (65%), Treasuries 6.5 (5%), small-business loans 54 (85%), fixed assets 12 (100%).
ask: Is the NSFR above or below the 100% minimum?

options.label: Above 100%
options.why: Compared unweighted funding (117.5) with the weighted RSF (82.9), mixing a raw total with a weighted one. Both sides must be weighted: $ASF = 80.25$.

takeaway: Weight both sides. Here wholesale funding at 50% pulls ASF just under RSF, so the NSFR is a shade below 100%.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Exim Bank: high-quality liquid assets USD 140m, estimated net cash outflows over the next 30 days USD 155m, stable funding USD 100m, capital USD 10m, total exposure USD 150m.
ask: Does the bank meet the Basel III minimum liquidity coverage ratio of 100%?

options.label: Yes: LCR is above 1
options.why: Inverted the ratio: $155/140 = 1.107$. The LCR has HQLA on top, outflows underneath.

takeaway: LCR is HQLA over 30-day net outflows. Stable funding, capital and exposure belong to other ratios (NSFR, leverage) and are distractors here.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: A bank reports (USD): HQLA 236, marketable securities 107, 30-day cash inflows 214, 30-day cash outflows 487, required stable funding 320, available stable funding 305, long-term economic capital 640.
ask: The 30-day net cash outflow used in the LCR denominator is closest to:

options.label: USD 487
options.why: Ignored the inflows. The denominator is outflows net of inflows.

options.label: USD 701
options.why: Added the inflows to the outflows instead of netting them.

takeaway: LCR denominator is outflows minus inflows over 30 days. The RSF, ASF and capital figures are for NSFR, not LCR.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: LCR inputs (USD m): Treasuries 90, counted in full; corporate debt 40, which counts after a 50% haircut; stable retail deposits 500 with 5% run-off; non-financial wholesale funding 300 with 40% run-off; expected 30-day inflows 60.
ask: High-quality liquid assets (HQLA) are closest to:

options.label: USD 90m
options.why: Left out the corporate debt altogether. After the 50% haircut it still contributes 20.

options.label: USD 130m
options.why: Counted the corporate debt at full value and ignored the 50% haircut.

takeaway: A haircut reduces what counts as HQLA; it does not remove the asset. Net outflows are run-offs less inflows.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel III leverage ratio. Tier 1 capital USD 250m, Tier 2 capital USD 150m, on-balance-sheet assets USD 2,000m (unweighted), off-balance-sheet loan commitments USD 300m entering the exposure measure at full face value.
ask: Is the leverage ratio above or below 12%?

options.label: Above 12%
options.why: Either left the commitments out of the exposure (250/2,000 = 12.5%) or counted Tier 2 capital in the numerator (400/2,300 = 17.4%). The ratio uses Tier 1 only, over assets plus commitments.

takeaway: Leverage ratio is Tier 1 over total (unweighted) exposure, including off-balance-sheet items. Tier 2 does not count.

reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
setup: A G-SIB faces a 2.0% risk-weighted higher-loss-absorbency (HLA) surcharge. Its leverage exposure measure is USD 800bn.
ask: Under the Basel III reforms the G-SIB leverage-ratio buffer, as a percentage of leverage exposure, is:

options.why: Halved the HLA twice. The buffer is 50% of the HLA requirement, applied once.
Carried the HLA surcharge straight across to the leverage ratio. The leverage buffer is only half of it.

takeaway: G-SIB leverage buffer = 50% of the risk-weighted HLA requirement, met with Tier 1 capital.

reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
setup: Basel III output floor, fully phased in at 72.5% of standardised-approach RWA. A bank's RWA from its approved internal models is USD 600bn; the same exposures under standardised approaches give USD 900bn.
ask: Is the output floor binding, so that regulatory RWA is above USD 600bn?

options.label: Yes: the floor, about USD 650bn, sets RWA
No: model RWA of USD 600bn stands
options.why: Applied 72.5% to the bank's own model RWA ($0.725 \times 600 = 435$), which looks harmless. The floor is a share of the standardised figure: $0.725 \times 900 = 652.5$.

takeaway: Output floor: RWA = max(model RWA, 72.5% of standardised RWA). It binds when models give more than 27.5% less than the standardised approach.
